about: Open problems whose solution would most likely matter beyond mathematics: algorithms and AI, communication and storage, quantum technology, physics and engineering, security. An editorial selection, not a measurement: each entry says why. Suggestions and corrections welcome on GitHub.

items.why: Whether every problem whose solutions are quick to check is also quick to solve. Modern cryptography assumes not; optimization, scheduling and AI would change completely if yes.
Matrix multiplication sits under scientific computing, graphics and every neural network. ω = 2 would mean multiplying matrices about as fast as reading them.
Whether randomness ever really helps algorithms. A proof would turn randomized algorithms used for testing, sampling and verification into deterministic ones.
Decides the best possible approximation guarantees for clustering, scheduling, network design and many other optimization problems.
Hundreds of lower bounds in algorithms and computational geometry rest on it; settling it tells engineers which speedups to stop looking for, or opens them.
Recognising when two networks, circuits or molecules have the same structure: chemical databases, circuit verification, network analysis.
Related to how many steps interior-point methods need to solve linear programs, the workhorse of logistics, planning and resource allocation.
Would imply efficient learning algorithms for broad classes of Boolean functions, a central question of computational learning theory.
The basic model of two wireless links sharing the same spectrum: its capacity region bounds what cellular and Wi-Fi networks can achieve.
One transmitter, two receivers (a base station serving two phones): the exact limits of downlink communication.
Capacity when a helper node forwards the signal: mesh networks, satellite and cellular relays.
Capacity when symbols disappear without notice: synchronization errors in communication, and DNA data storage.
Describes everything network coding and distributed storage systems can achieve; known only for three or fewer variables.
Zero-error communication over a noisy channel; the 7-cycle is the smallest case nobody can compute.
Hadamard matrices give error-correcting codes, CDMA spreading sequences and optimal experimental designs; the conjecture says one exists in every size divisible by 4.
The densest packings are the best signal constellations and lattice codes for communication; solved only in dimensions 1, 2, 3, 8 and 24.
Spherical codes: how many signals can be kept a fixed distance apart, used in coding for communication channels.
Mutually unbiased bases underpin quantum key distribution and quantum state tomography. Whether 7 of them exist in dimension 6, the smallest case that is not a prime power, is open.
Absolutely maximally entangled states give quantum error-correcting codes and quantum secret-sharing schemes.
Complex Hadamard matrices are used to build unitary error bases in quantum information and in signal design.
Whether the equations used for air and water can break down. They are behind every simulation of weather, aircraft, engines and blood flow. Millennium Prize.
The frictionless version of the same question; blow-up is tied to how turbulence forms.
A rigorous foundation for the theory of the strong force, which explains why protons and neutrons have mass. Millennium Prize.
Bounds the gaps between consecutive primes, which governs how quickly cryptographic software can find the large primes it needs.
